experiments.title: Fire on a synced schedule, or react to the signal?
experiments.hypothesis: Firing at a clock-synced launch instant lands closer to the release than reacting to the live signal, because a reactor first pays a detect round-trip.
experiments.method: Same warm-connection bot, one variable: reactive long-polls then fires; proactive syncs to /api/server-time and fires at the launch instant, retrying if the server flips late. Loopback.
experiments.conclusion: Proactive wins — ~20% lower median (proactive ~0.87 vs reactive ~1.10 ms). Firing at the synced launch instant skips the detect round-trip a reactor pays. On loopback that round-trip is tiny so the edge is modest; it scales with network RTT, where proactive can beat a reactor by nearly a full round-trip.
experiments.decision: Fire proactively at the clock-synced launch, keeping a reactive long-poll as backup — first success wins.

experiments.title: Does pre-warming the connection actually help?
experiments.hypothesis: A pre-warmed keep-alive socket beats opening the connection at fire time, because the TCP handshake is paid before the drop instead of inside the fire window.
experiments.method: Same HTTP-direct bot, one variable: warm pre-opens the fire socket before the drop; cold opens it after detecting release. Loopback, single-clock release->hit.
experiments.conclusion: Pre-warming wins — ~26% lower median (warm ~1.10 vs cold ~1.48 ms). Even on loopback, where a TCP connect is nearly free, opening the socket inside the fire window still costs ~0.4 ms. On a real TLS endpoint that gap is a full handshake (tens of ms), so warming is decisive.
experiments.decision: Always pre-warm the fire connection before the drop; cold-connect is never worth it.

experiments.title: Browser automation vs raw HTTP — the cost of a real click
experiments.hypothesis: Firing the raw request (HTTP-direct / hybrid) is materially faster than driving a real browser click.
experiments.method: Approach A (Playwright MutationObserver click), B (raw HTTP-direct, Rust), and C (hybrid: real browser, injected fetch) race the same mock; release→hit on one clock.
experiments.conclusion: Raw HTTP is ~4-5x faster than a rendered click, and the hybrid beats the observer by skipping the render->observe->click chain. Browser tails are also much fatter (p95).
experiments.decision: Default to C for a real drop (browser cover + near-raw speed); drop to B only with a known endpoint and no CAPTCHA.

experiments.title: Rust vs Python — the HTTP-direct floor
experiments.hypothesis: A compiled language (Rust) posts a lower firing floor than Python for the HTTP-direct approach.
experiments.method: Ran approach_b_http in each language, 30 trials, against the local mock on loopback; scored release→hit on the server's single monotonic clock.
experiments.conclusion: Rust posts the lower floor (~0.7 vs ~1.0 ms median), but both HTTP-direct langs cluster within ~1 ms — the approach dominates the language.
experiments.decision: Publish Rust as the record floor; keep Python for day-to-day iteration.
